screens.title: Setting Up Your Plutus Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you'll set up a development environment that avoids the classic "works on my machine" problem. We use Nix because it builds packages in isolation and produces reproducible environments. That matters for Plutus development where exact compiler, library, and tool versions affect contract behavior. You'll learn how to install Nix, verify it, clone the Plutus starter repository, enter the nix-shell, and compile a basic contract with cabal build. You'll also learn practical troubleshooting tips and maintenance commands to manage disk space. For example, we'll show the commands you'll run and explain why the first nix-shell invocation takes a long time: Nix may build GHC and libraries from source, so patience is required. We'll highlight common mistakes, like running cabal build outside the nix-shell, and how to confirm your prompt changes when inside the environment. By the end, you'll be able to reproduce a working Plutus toolchain on any supported machine and restart work safely after updates. Think about the last time a dependency mismatch derailed a build; this approach prevents that and makes collaboration predictable. Are you ready to make your development reproducible and reliable?

screens.narratorSegment: These objectives describe what you'll be able to do after completing the setup. First, you will install and configure Nix so you can create reproducible development environments. This skill matters because Plutus development requires exact tool versions; if you can install Nix correctly, you remove a major source of build variation. Second, you will clone and navigate the official Plutus starter repository. Knowing how to fetch and inspect the starter project lets you study example contracts and the provided shell. nix file. Third, you will use nix-shell to enter a pre-configured environment; you'll understand that this command loads specific GHC and Cabal versions so builds are consistent across machines. Fourth, you will be able to compile a basic Plutus contract with cabal build while inside the nix-shell and troubleshoot common errors, such as running cabal outside the shell or missing PATH updates. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can self-check your competency. Practice each step slowly: a successful initial build and a working cabal output is a clear signal you've achieved the goals. Keep these objectives in mind as you progress through the hands-on steps and troubleshooting guidance.

screens.title: How you'll use these skills
screens.narratorSegment: In this slide we map each objective to a practical checkpoint. Installing Nix is validated by running nix --version and restarting your shell, which confirms the environment variables are correct. Cloning the Plutus starter repository is validated when you can list the project files and open shell. nix; this helps you inspect pinned dependencies. Entering nix-shell is validated by the environment prompt changing or by running ghc --version inside the shell and seeing the expected compiler version. Compiling a contract is validated by a successful cabal build output indicating packages were built without missing dependencies. A useful mnemonic is PATH-GC: PATH to remember shell PATH changes, G for GHC version check, and C for cabal build confirmation; GC reminds you to garbage collect the Nix store periodically. We'll pair each checkpoint with a small verification command so you can self-assess quickly. Finally, we note common pitfalls — forgetting to restart a shell or running cabal outside of nix-shell — and how to check for them. These checkpoints help you progress from installing tools to reliably compiling Plutus code.

screens.title: What is Nix and why Plutus uses it
screens.narratorSegment: Nix is a functional package manager that builds dependencies in isolation and records exact build inputs so environment outputs are reproducible. In practice, this means packages are defined as pure functions of their inputs, which prevents system-level dependency conflicts. For Plutus development, reproducibility is non-negotiable because smart contracts must behave consistently across machines and over time. A small example: two developers compiling the same Plutus contract with slightly different GHC versions may produce different binary artifacts or face subtle type errors. Using Nix removes that variance by pinning compiler and library versions inside a project-specific configuration, typically expressed in shell. nix or flake files. A common misconception is that Nix simply installs packages like a conventional package manager. It does more: it creates isolated, repeatable builds and a local store of immutable package builds. Another misconception is that Nix is only for Linux; while multi-platform support exists, follow platform-specific guidance when installing. To verify you understand the concept, try describing why an isolated GHC leads to fewer build errors. Takeaway: Nix turns environment configuration into code, making Plutus builds predictable and sharable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What is Nix
Nix: a functional package manager
Nix builds packages in isolation and records exact inputs so outputs are reproducible.
Definition
Packages are functions of inputs; builds are deterministic and stored immutably.
Why Plutus uses it
Ensures all developers use the exact same GHC, Cabal, and library versions to avoid subtle contract differences.
Concrete example
Two developers use different system GHCs and see a mismatch. Nix pins the GHC used by the project and prevents that mismatch.
Common misconception
Nix is not just a smarter installer. It's an isolation and reproducibility system for full build environments.
Key takeaway
Treat environment configuration as code so builds are predictable across machines and time.

screens.title: Install Nix on your system
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Nix is the first practical step. The usual flow is: run the official installer command, follow prompts, restart or source your shell profile, then verify the installation with nix --version. Use the installer command exactly as provided by the project maintainers; in many cases you paste a single curl pipeline that runs the installer script. After installation, a common pitfall is forgetting to restart the terminal or to source your shell profile, which means the Nix binary won't appear in your PATH and commands like nix --version fail. Another pitfall is insufficient disk space; Nix stores packages in its own store, which can grow quickly when compiling GHC and libraries. Verification steps include running nix --version and checking that the store directory exists. If the installer reports permission issues, ensure you followed the correct single-user or multi-user installation instructions for your OS. As an example, after running the installer you should see a printed version. If not, reopen your terminal, run the shell profile source command for your shell, and try again. Takeaway: installation is straightforward but pay attention to PATH and disk space.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Install Nix
Install Nix
Run the official installer, then verify the binary is in your PATH and that nix --version outputs a version string.
Step-by-step
  1. Run the installer command provided by Nix maintainers.
  2. Follow prompts and choose multi-user mode when appropriate.
  3. Restart your terminal or source your shell profile.
  4. Run nix --version to verify installation.
Common pitfalls
Not restarting the shell, insufficient disk space, or permission errors during a multi-user install.
Installer example (terminal)
curl -L https://nixos.org/nix/install | sh
# Follow prompts, then restart your terminal or source your shell profile
nix --version
If nix --version does not print, re-open your terminal and check your shell profile for the Nix initialization line.
Example result
A successful install prints a Nix version and makes the nix command available globally for your user.
Takeaway
Install carefully, verify PATH changes, and ensure enough disk space before long builds.

screens.title: Clone the Plutus starter project
screens.narratorSegment: Cloning the Plutus starter repository gives you a pre-configured project with a shell. nix file that defines the development environment. Start by choosing a comfortable work directory, then run git clone followed by cd into the newly created directory. The shell. nix file is the contract between your project and Nix; it lists the exact packages and versions Nix should compose when you run nix-shell. Inspect shell. nix with a text editor so you understand which GHC and Plutus libraries are pinned. A practical check is to list files and open the cabal. project or. cabal file to see build targets that cabal will use. Common mistakes include cloning to a path with spaces or insufficient permissions, which can confuse some build scripts; use a simple path like ~/dev/plutus-starter. Another common issue is forgetting to fetch submodules if the repository relies on them — check the project README for instructions. Example commands to run are straightforward: git clone https://github. com/input-output-hk/plutus-starter. git and cd plutus-starter. After cloning and inspection, you're ready to run nix-shell. The takeaway: cloning gives you a reproducible starting point so you don't configure the environment manually.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Clone the starter project
Clone the Plutus starter project
Fetch the official repository to get a pre-built project with environment definitions and example contracts.
Commands
git clone https://github.com/input-output-hk/plutus-starter.git
cd plutus-starter
ls -la
Open shell.nix and cabal.project to inspect pinned packages and build targets.
What to inspect
  • shell.nix: pinned GHC and libraries.
  • cabal.project: build targets and package paths.
  • README: repo-specific instructions and possible submodules.
Example scenario
Cloning to a path with spaces may break scripts. Choose a clean path like ~/dev/plutus-starter.
Takeaway
Cloning gives you a reproducible scaffold; inspect shell.nix before entering the shell.

screens.title: Entering nix-shell
screens.narratorSegment: When you run nix-shell inside the cloned project, Nix reads shell. nix and composes the specified environment. The first invocation often takes a long time because Nix may need to download and build large dependencies from source, including the Glasgow Haskell Compiler and Plutus libraries. This is normal. You will see a stream of output as Nix fetches packages and compiles them. The shell ends by starting a subshell with environment variables and PATH modified so that local GHC and Cabal are used. A key confirmation is the prompt change or running ghc --version within the shell and seeing the pinned version. A common misconception is thinking nix-shell downloads only prebuilt binaries; sometimes it must build from source, especially when pinned versions or derivations are specific. If the process seems stuck, check network activity and disk input and output; Nix is often still working. After the initial setup, subsequent nix-shell entries are faster because the Nix store caches built artifacts. Example: run nix-shell once, wait through compilation, then run ghc --version and cabal --version to verify. Takeaway: expect a long first run, but trust that caching will speed up later work.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Entering nix-shell
Enter the nix-shell
Run nix-shell to create an environment with pinned GHC and Cabal. Expect long initial builds.
What to expect
  • Downloading and building dependencies, possibly including GHC.
  • Long terminal output; be patient — it is usually working.
  • Final prompt indicates you are inside the shell with correct PATH.
Quick checks
Run ghc --version and cabal --version inside the shell to confirm pinned versions.
Terminal example
nix-shell
# lengthy download and build output...
# after completion, prompt changes
ghc --version
cabal --version
If the build seems stuck, check your internet connection and disk usage; Nix may still be compiling in the background.
Misconception
nix-shell always downloads prebuilt binaries. In practice, Nix may build from source depending on derivations and caches.
Takeaway
Be patient on first run; caching makes later shells fast and predictable.

screens.title: Build a basic Plutus contract with cabal
screens.narratorSegment: Once you're inside the nix-shell, the standard way to compile Haskell-based Plutus code is with cabal build. Cabal reads cabal. project and package files to resolve build targets and compile them using the GHC available in the shell. A concrete example: after entering nix-shell, run cabal build. During the build you will see package configuration, dependency resolution, compilation steps, and linking. Successful output indicates compiled packages and created artifacts; errors commonly point to missing dependencies or mismatched versions. One common user mistake is trying to run cabal build from the host shell without being inside nix-shell; in that case cabal may not be installed or may use a different GHC, producing errors. Another issue is low disk space causing failed builds mid-way; monitor disk capacity during long builds. After a successful build, inspect the local dist or build directory to find compiled artifacts. Finally, if build logs are long, search for 'Warning' or 'Error' lines rather than scanning everything manually. Takeaway: cabal build is the validated way to compile Plutus code inside a pinned environment; ensure you're inside nix-shell before running it.

keyIdea.text: Run cabal build after entering nix-shell. If cabal fails, confirm you're in the nix-shell and monitor disk and network conditions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Build with cabal
Compile with cabal build
Run cabal build inside the nix-shell to compile Plutus and off-chain code with the pinned toolchain.
Terminal walkthrough
nix-shell
# once inside the shell
cabal build
# observe configuration, compilation, and linking output
# on success, artifacts appear in the build/dist directory
Common error
Running cabal outside nix-shell yields missing cabal or GHC errors; re-enter nix-shell and retry.
Pro tip
Search build logs for 'error' and 'warning' to quickly locate real issues in long output.
Example outcome
On success you'll see package build summaries and created build artifacts. If the build fails, copy the first error block to diagnose the cause.
Key Takeaway

Always run cabal build inside nix-shell. Confirm the correct GHC and Cabal versions with --version checks inside the shell.

screens.title: Inside vs outside nix-shell
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between your host shell and nix-shell is crucial. Inside nix-shell, environment variables, PATH entries, and installed tools are those specified by shell. nix. Outside, the system uses whatever GHC, Cabal, and libraries your OS provides. A concrete example: running ghc --version outside the shell might show a system compiler that is several versions off. Running the same command inside nix-shell should show the pinned version. This discrepancy explains many mysterious build failures. A common misconception is that nix-shell permanently changes your system environment — it does not. It creates a temporary subshell; typing exit returns you to your normal shell. To check where a binary is being resolved from, use which ghc or type ghc in the shell; compare results inside and outside nix-shell. If you find that cabal resolves to a different binary than expected, re-enter nix-shell and rerun the commands. Takeaway: always confirm the toolchain version inside nix-shell before building, and treat the shell as the authoritative environment for Plutus work. Inside vs outside nix-shell means nix-shell provides a temporary, pinned environment. confirm tool versions inside the shell to avoid host-system mismatches.. In practical terms, why commands behave differently and how to check your environment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Inside vs outside nix-shell
Inside vs outside nix-shell
Compare how commands resolve between your normal shell and the nix-shell to avoid confusion.
Quick check commands
# outside shell
which ghc
# inside nix-shell
nix-shell
which ghc
ghc --version
Example contrast
Outside: ghc -> /usr/bin/ghc (system version). Inside: ghc -> /nix/store/.../bin/ghc (pinned version). This difference explains many build issues.
Common mistake
Running cabal build outside the nix-shell and wondering why dependencies are missing.
Key Takeaway

Treat nix-shell as the canonical environment. Always confirm tool versions inside it before compiling.

screens.title: Exiting the shell and workflow tips
screens.narratorSegment: Exiting nix-shell is simple—type exit or press Ctrl+D. When you do, the temporary environment is torn down and your PATH returns to the host values. A practical workflow is to cd into the project, run nix-shell, perform builds and tests, then exit when done. Frequent tasks inside the shell include running cabal build, running tests, and interacting with local simulator tooling if present. Keep a short checklist: ensure you're in the project directory, run nix-shell, verify ghc and cabal versions, then run cabal build. For iterative development, keeping a small terminal session open with the shell can speed up cycles, but remember to exit when you want to switch contexts. A common misconception is that exiting the shell deletes the Nix store — it does not. The built artifacts remain in the Nix store; the shell only provided access to them. Finally, be cautious when updating the repository or the shell. nix: after pulling changes, rerun nix-shell to pick up new pinned dependencies. Takeaway: cothere is a predictable loop—enter nix-shell, work, exit—so you always use the project's pinned toolchain. screens.title: Common issues during setup and their fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Setup can fail for a few predictable reasons. Permission issues during installation often arise from selecting the wrong installer mode or missing administrative privileges. If you see permission errors, re-run the installer following the recommended mode for your OS and ensure you follow multi-user vs single-user guidance. Missing PATH entries usually mean you need to restart the terminal or source your shell profile; check that the Nix initialization lines have been added to ~/. bashrc or ~/. zshrc and run source ~/. bashrc as needed. Long builds are usually normal on first run; however, if the process truly stalls, check network connectivity and disk space. Use system tools to inspect disk input and output; a high input and output or full disk is a likely cause of failure. Another frequent problem is running cabal build outside the nix-shell — the fix is to cd into the project and run nix-shell first. If a build fails mid-way with obscure error messages, copy the earliest error block and search for that specific message or consult the repository README for version constraints. As a maintenance step, periodically run nix-collect-garbage -d to reclaim disk space left by old builds. Takeaway: many errors have straightforward fixes—check permissions, PATH, disk space, and whether you're inside the nix-shell.

screens.title: Managing disk space and cleaning the Nix store
screens.narratorSegment: Nix stores package builds in the Nix store, which can grow large over time as you build multiple projects or update dependencies. Periodically reclaiming unused artifacts prevents disk exhaustion. The recommended command to reclaim space is nix-collect-garbage -d, which removes old, unreferenced store paths. Before running destructive commands, check which store paths are referenced by current profiles or generations. Use nix-store --gc --print-roots carefully if you need detailed answers. A practical pattern is to run nix-collect-garbage periodically or after major upgrades, especially if you see free disk space dropping below comfortable thresholds. A common misconception is that uninstalling a package with a normal package manager will free Nix store files; it will not—Nix keeps immutable store paths until you garbage collect them. Another maintenance tip is to limit build artifacts by using shared caches or binary substitutes when available. Example: when you finish active development on a project that consumed large builds, run nix-collect-garbage -d to free space, but be aware you may need to rebuild artifacts later if you re-enter older projects. Takeaway: garbage collection keeps your machine usable but remember it permanently removes unreferenced artifacts.

Welcome. In this lesson you'll set up a development environment that avoids the classic "works on my machine" problem. We use Nix because it builds packages in isolation and produces reproducible environments. That matters for Plutus development where exact compiler, library, and tool versions affect contract behavior. You'll learn how to install Nix, verify it, clone the Plutus starter repository, enter the nix-shell, and compile a basic contract with cabal build. You'll also learn practical troubleshooting tips and maintenance commands to manage disk space. For example, we'll show the commands you'll run and explain why the first nix-shell invocation takes a long time: Nix may build GHC and libraries from source, so patience is required. We'll highlight common mistakes, like running cabal build outside the nix-shell, and how to confirm your prompt changes when inside the environment. By the end, you'll be able to reproduce a working Plutus toolchain on any supported machine and restart work safely after updates. Think about the last time a dependency mismatch derailed a build; this approach prevents that and makes collaboration predictable. Are you ready to make your development reproducible and reliable?

These objectives describe what you'll be able to do after completing the setup. First, you will install and configure Nix so you can create reproducible development environments. This skill matters because Plutus development requires exact tool versions; if you can install Nix correctly, you remove a major source of build variation. Second, you will clone and navigate the official Plutus starter repository. Knowing how to fetch and inspect the starter project lets you study example contracts and the provided shell. nix file. Third, you will use nix-shell to enter a pre-configured environment; you'll understand that this command loads specific GHC and Cabal versions so builds are consistent across machines. Fourth, you will be able to compile a basic Plutus contract with cabal build while inside the nix-shell and troubleshoot common errors, such as running cabal outside the shell or missing PATH updates. Each objective includes a verification milestone so you can self-check your competency. Practice each step slowly: a successful initial build and a working cabal output is a clear signal you've achieved the goals. Keep these objectives in mind as you progress through the hands-on steps and troubleshooting guidance.

In this slide we map each objective to a practical checkpoint. Installing Nix is validated by running nix --version and restarting your shell, which confirms the environment variables are correct. Cloning the Plutus starter repository is validated when you can list the project files and open shell. nix; this helps you inspect pinned dependencies. Entering nix-shell is validated by the environment prompt changing or by running ghc --version inside the shell and seeing the expected compiler version. Compiling a contract is validated by a successful cabal build output indicating packages were built without missing dependencies. A useful mnemonic is PATH-GC: PATH to remember shell PATH changes, G for GHC version check, and C for cabal build confirmation; GC reminds you to garbage collect the Nix store periodically. We'll pair each checkpoint with a small verification command so you can self-assess quickly. These checkpoints help you progress from installing tools to reliably compiling Plutus code.

Nix is a functional package manager that builds dependencies in isolation and records exact build inputs so environment outputs are reproducible. In practice, this means packages are defined as pure functions of their inputs, which prevents system-level dependency conflicts. For Plutus development, reproducibility is non-negotiable because smart contracts must behave consistently across machines and over time. A small example: two developers compiling the same Plutus contract with slightly different GHC versions may produce different binary artifacts or face subtle type errors. Using Nix removes that variance by pinning compiler and library versions inside a project-specific configuration, typically expressed in shell. nix or flake files. A common misconception is that Nix simply installs packages like a conventional package manager. It does more: it creates isolated, repeatable builds and a local store of immutable package builds. Another misconception is that Nix is only for Linux; while multi-platform support exists, follow platform-specific guidance when installing. To verify you understand the concept, try describing why an isolated GHC leads to fewer build errors. Takeaway: Nix turns environment configuration into code, making Plutus builds predictable and sharable.

Installing Nix is the first practical step. The usual flow is: run the official installer command, follow prompts, restart or source your shell profile, then verify the installation with nix --version. Use the installer command exactly as provided by the project maintainers; in many cases you paste a single curl pipeline that runs the installer script. After installation, a common pitfall is forgetting to restart the terminal or to source your shell profile, which means the Nix binary won't appear in your PATH and commands like nix --version fail. Another pitfall is insufficient disk space; Nix stores packages in its own store, which can grow quickly when compiling GHC and libraries. If the installer reports permission issues, ensure you followed the correct single-user or multi-user installation instructions for your OS. As an example, after running the installer you should see a printed version. If not, reopen your terminal, run the shell profile source command for your shell, and try again. Takeaway: installation is straightforward but pay attention to PATH and disk space.

Cloning the Plutus starter repository gives you a pre-configured project with a shell. nix file that defines the development environment. Start by choosing a comfortable work directory, then run git clone followed by cd into the newly created directory. Before running destructive commands, check which store paths are referenced by current profiles or generations. Use nix-store --gc --print-roots carefully if you need detailed answers. A practical pattern is to run nix-collect-garbage periodically or after major upgrades, especially if you see free disk space dropping below comfortable thresholds. A common misconception is that uninstalling a package with a normal package manager will free Nix store files; it will not—Nix keeps immutable store paths until you garbage collect them. Another maintenance tip is to limit build artifacts by using shared caches or binary substitutes when available. Example: when you finish active development on a project that consumed large builds, run nix-collect-garbage -d to free space, but be aware you may need to rebuild artifacts later if you re-enter older projects. Takeaway: garbage collection keeps your machine usable but remember it permanently removes unreferenced artifacts.
